title: Fisherman's rib beanie
subtitle: A thick fisherman's rib beanie in aran yarn, three adult sizes.
excerpt: A bottom-up fisherman's rib beanie in aran yarn, worked in the round on 5 mm needles. The slip-stitch rib creates a double-thick, deeply cushioned fabric that holds its shape after repeated washing.
sourceNotes: Fisherman's rib as a hat fabric draws on Barbara Walker's Treasury of Knitting Patterns Vol 2 (1970) and Elizabeth Zimmermann's Knitter's Almanac (1974).

glossaryTerms.definition: A method of knitting a small circumference on one long circular needle by pulling a loop of cable through the work at the halfway point.

A slip-stitch rib worked in the round: on every round, purl stitches are worked normally and knit stitches are slipped with yarn in back, creating a double-thick elastic fabric identical in appearance to brioche rib.

content.text: This fisherman's rib beanie is worked bottom-up in the round, fitting adult heads of 54 (56, 58) cm.
Bottom-up construction keeps the rib columns straight from cast-on to crown.
Fisherman's rib

is worked by slipping every knit stitch with yarn in back instead of knitting it: the result looks identical to brioche rib but requires no yarn-over setup row, which keeps the construction clean in the round. The fabric is double-thick and cushioned -- noticeably warmer than standard 2 x 2 rib from the same yarn. The
magic loop
method works the full hat on one needle. About 120 g (215 m) of aran yarn. Sits at the brow line and does not ride up on the back of the head.
What you need

items.name: 4.5 mm circular needle, 80 cm (UK 7 / US 7) -- for the brim

content.text: Gauge

16 sts x 22 rounds = 10 x 10 cm in fisherman's rib (relaxed, not stretched) on 5 mm needles. Swatch in the round: cast on 32 sts, join, work several rounds of fisherman's rib, and measure relaxed off the needle. At 17 sts per 10 cm the crown circumference for size S closes at about 52 cm relaxed -- the hat will fit but sit tight on a 54 cm head. Gauge matters more here than on a plain rib because the slipped stitches compress the fabric further than usual.
Stitches used
k -- knit
p -- purl
sl1 wyib -- slip 1 stitch purlwise with yarn in back
k2tog -- knit two stitches together (right-leaning decrease)
Pattern
Before you cast on, circle your size -- every count reads S (M, L).
Cast on
Using
magic loop

on the 4.5 mm needle, cast on 88 (92, 96) sts using long-tail cast-on. The cast-on count must be a multiple of 4 so the k1 p1 pattern sits correctly. Tail formula: tail_cm = (needle mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For size L on a 4.5 mm needle: (4.5 x 96) / 10 + 15 = 58 cm; round up to 65 cm. Join without twisting, place BOR marker.
Brim
Work 8 rounds of k1 p1 rib on the 4.5 mm needle. Switch to 5 mm needle. After completing the brim, you should have 88 (92, 96) stitches on the needle.
Fisherman's rib body

Fisherman's rib round: *sl1 wyib, p1; repeat from * to end. Repeat this round only -- every round is the same. Work until hat measures 22 cm from cast-on edge. The slipped stitches build up slowly; do not be alarmed if the round count looks low for the measurement.
Crown shaping
Switch from fisherman's rib to plain knit for the decrease rounds -- this keeps the decreases clean. Place 8 markers evenly dividing the work into 8 sections of 11 (11.5, 12) sts.
Decrease round 1: *k to 2 sts before marker, k2tog; repeat from * 8 times. 80 (84, 88) sts.
Round 2: knit all.
Decrease round 3: *k to 2 sts before marker, k2tog; repeat from * 8 times. 72 (76, 80) sts.
Round 4: knit all.
Continue alternating decrease and plain rounds, removing markers as sections shrink, until 32 sts remain.
Final rounds: decrease every round until 8 sts remain.
After the final decrease round, you should have 8 stitches on the needle, ready to gather.
Top finish
Cut yarn with 20 cm tail. Draw tail through all 8 sts, slide off the needle, and pull up firmly. Fasten off on the inside.
Common faults

Fabric looks like ordinary k1 p1 rib: the slipped stitch is being knitted instead of slipped. Check yarn is held in back (wyib) before slipping; the stitch moves right needle to left without the yarn wrapping over it.

Round count required to reach height is double what the pattern says: fisherman's rib builds at roughly half the row-height rate of stockinette because every stitch is worked on alternate rounds. This is correct behaviour, not a gauge problem.
Crown puckers at the decrease columns: decreases started mid-section or markers slipped accidentally. Count stitches per section before the first decrease round and adjust if uneven.
Brim rolls outward: the k1 p1 brim section is too short or was worked on too large a needle. The brim wants 4 cm minimum depth on the smaller needle before switching.
Finishing
Weave in both ends. Wet-block lightly over a hat form or bowl: the fisherman's rib will compact further when wet-blocked and spring back fully on drying.
Care
Hand wash cool in wool wash. Squeeze gently without wringing. Reshape and dry flat away from direct heat.
What to try next
The brioche beret uses the same slipped-stitch principle. It widens to a deep dish shape before the crown decreases, giving a very different silhouette.
